opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's less about which route is right and more about where each one hits a wall first.

Teleoperation has a very concrete advantage: the data is real. The contact physics, the friction, the way a cable deforms or a towel bunches up, the small delays and noise in the sensors are all there, because you collected them on the actual hardware in an actual environment. For manipulation especially, the sim-to-real gap is not a detail. It's often the whole problem. So if your goal is to get a robot doing a specific job in a specific factory or warehouse in the next year or two, teleoperated data is probably the faster path. You collect a few hundred or a few thousand demonstrations, you train a policy, and it works well enough to deploy in that narrow setting. Many companies are doing exactly that right now.

The problem is scaling. Teleoperation is expensive in a very linear way: one operator, one robot, one episode at a time. Language models had the whole internet. We have nothing like that for physical interaction, and you can't build an internet's worth of robot data with people wearing VR headsets. There's also a diversity issue. Operators tend to repeat similar strategies, and you rarely capture the failures and recoveries that make a policy robust. And the data is tied to a particular embodiment, so when you change the gripper or the arm, part of what you collected loses value.

Synthetic data addresses exactly those weaknesses. Simulation is cheap to scale, you can randomize environments endlessly, you can deliberately generate edge cases and failures, and you can switch embodiments relatively easily. For locomotion, it has basically already won. Most of the impressive legged-robot results come from reinforcement learning in simulation. But for dexterous manipulation with deformable objects, liquids, and rich contact, simulators are still not faithful enough, and building good simulated assets and scenes is itself a big engineering cost people tend to underestimate.

So my view is that in the short term, teleoperated real data will deploy faster in narrow, commercially valuable scenarios. In the long term, I don't think any single source wins. The likely structure looks like a pyramid. At the bottom, a huge amount of cheap, weakly labeled data: human video, internet video, synthetic data, maybe world-model-generated data, which teaches general priors about how the world works. In the middle, simulation for scaling skills and covering the long tail. At the top, a relatively small amount of high-quality real teleoperation data to align the model to real physics and a real body.

The real competition, then, is about who builds the most efficient data flywheel. Once robots are deployed and working, every real interaction becomes data, and that matters more than whether you started with teleop or simulation. Teleop gets you to deployment sooner, and deployment is what eventually gets you the scale. Synthetic data determines how far the model can generalize beyond what you've physically collected. The teams that win will treat these as complementary rather than as competing camps.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the teleoperation route gets you to a visible deployment faster, but it doesn't necessarily get you to a scalable deployment faster, and those are two very different finish lines.

Let me break that down. If your goal is to have a robot doing a specific task in a specific factory or kitchen in six months, real teleoperated data is hard to beat. You put a human in the loop, you collect a few thousand demonstrations on the exact hardware, in the exact lighting, with the exact objects, and you train a policy. The distribution match is nearly perfect because you're literally collecting from the target distribution. There's no sim-to-real gap to argue about. You just ship. That's why so many of the companies that have actual paying customers right now are on this path.

The problem is what happens on task number two, and task number twenty. Teleoperation is fundamentally a labor cost that scales linearly with the amount of data you want. A skilled operator can maybe produce a few hundred useful episodes a day, and the quality varies a lot with the person. You can parallelize by hiring more people, and some companies in China are doing exactly that with data collection factories, but you're still paying per episode forever. You never get to the point where the marginal cost of data drops toward zero, which is the thing that made language models work.

Synthetic data has the opposite profile. The first six months are painful. You're building simulators, you're fighting with contact physics, you're discovering that your rendered textures teach the model things that don't transfer. Early results look worse than the teleop team's results, and investors notice. But if you get through that, the cost curve bends in a way the other route structurally cannot. You can generate a million variations of a grasp overnight. You can randomize object geometry, friction, lighting, camera position, all of it. And you can do it for tasks where human demonstration is slow or dangerous or just boring.

So my actual assessment is that the question "which is faster" is a little bit of a trap. The teams I think will win are the ones treating real data as the anchor and synthetic data as the amplifier. You use a relatively small amount of teleoperated data to calibrate the simulator, to learn what real contact and real sensor noise actually look like, and then you use the simulator to blow that out by a hundred or a thousand times. The real data tells you what the world is, the synthetic data gives you enough coverage to generalize.

Where I'd push back on the pure synthetic camp is that they tend to underestimate how much of robotics is in the long tail of physical weirdness. Deformable objects, liquids, transparent things, cables that tangle. Simulators are still bad at these, and those are exactly the things that break deployments. Where I'd push back on the pure teleop camp is that they're often building a very expensive dataset that's tied to one hardware generation. The moment you change the gripper or the camera, a surprising fraction of that data loses value.

One more thing I'd add, because I think it's underappreciated. Teleoperation data carries the operator's intent. When a human moves a robot arm, there's a reason behind every motion, even if the trajectory is suboptimal. Synthetic data generated from a planner tends to be geometrically clean but semantically empty. For learning manipulation skills, that intent signal turns out to matter more than people expected, and it's one reason why models trained on real demonstrations often feel more natural even when their raw success rates are similar.

So if you forced me to bet: teleop-centered teams deploy first, probably by a year or two, in narrow commercial settings. Synthetic-centered teams, if they survive long enough, deploy more broadly later. And the companies that actually end up dominating will be the ones that stopped treating it as a binary somewhere along the way.

astra-6.text:
I think teleoperated real data has an advantage in getting the first useful applications deployed, but I wouldn’t conclude that it will necessarily scale faster all the way through.

The advantage is that you’re collecting data on the actual robot, in the actual environment, with real contact and real failures. If you pick a relatively narrow task, teleoperation can help you establish what successful behavior looks like and get a policy working. You can then use human intervention to handle failures and collect examples of exactly where the policy needs improvement. That creates a practical loop between deployment and training.

But collecting more hours isn’t automatically the same as making progress. You need coverage of different situations, consistent demonstrations, and a way to capture recovery behavior. If humans have to intervene frequently, the cost of operating the system can limit how quickly you expand. So I’d look less at total data volume and more at whether intervention rates fall as you collect additional data.

Synthetic data has a different strength: you can generate variations and repeat difficult scenarios at scale. The question is whether those variations teach something that transfers to the physical robot. For tasks where contact dynamics matter a lot, that can be a substantial challenge.

So if the objective is to deploy a specific application sooner, I’d lean toward real data collected through teleoperation. If the objective is broad capability across many tasks and environments, I wouldn’t bet on teleoperation alone. The promising route is to use real deployment experience to identify what’s missing, and then use synthetic data wherever it can reliably fill those gaps. The decisive measure is how quickly you improve autonomous task success at an acceptable cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think teleoperated real data is likely to get us to useful deployments faster in the near term, especially when the task and environment are relatively well defined. It gives you examples that already contain the realities of contact, friction, occlusion, and recovery from mistakes. Those are precisely the things that are difficult to reproduce faithfully in simulation.

But collecting real data is not automatically the same as collecting useful data. If operators repeat successful demonstrations under ideal conditions, you can accumulate a lot of hours without teaching the robot how to handle failures. The important questions are how much diversity you capture, whether the observations and actions are consistent, and whether the data actually improves autonomous performance.

Synthetic data has a different advantage: you can vary environments and generate difficult cases at scale. But its value depends on whether those variations transfer to the real world. A model can look very capable in simulation and still fail on a small physical detail.

So I would distinguish getting the first deployment from scaling to many deployments. For the first, I would put more weight on teleoperated real data. For scaling, I would expect a combination: use real deployments to identify what the system cannot do, use simulation and synthetic data to expand coverage, and then validate on the robot. The decisive advantage is how quickly that loop improves reliability and reduces the need for human intervention.
